background.definition: Pericarditis is a syndrome of active pericardial inflammation characterized by the clinical triad of pleuritic chest pain, pericardial friction rub, and diffuse electrocardiographic ST-T wave elevation.

list.listitem: Among patients hospitalized with chest pain, pericarditis is infrequent, occurring in less than 1% of patients.
Approximately 5% of emergency department patients with chest pain symptoms and no evidence of myocardial infarction have pericarditis.
Male to female ratio is 3:1 in high income countries.

Ninety percent of cases in the developed world are either viral or idiopathic. Common etiologic viruses include enterovirus, echovirus, adenovirus, cytomegalovirus, Ebstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus, influenza, parvovirus B19, hepatitis C, SARS-CoV-2, dengue virus, and HIV. After viral or idiopathic etiology, the second most common cause is acute pericaditis due to cardiac procedures or surgeries.
The most common cause in low income countries is tuberculosis.

Additional causes include myocardial infarction, bacterial infections, uremia, dissecting ascending aortic aneurysm, neoplasm, thoracic surgery, non-penetrating chest trauma, mediastinal radiation, autoimmune diseases, and rarely, adverse drug reactions.
Pericardial inflammation may result from direct viral attack or as a result of antiviral or anticardiac cellular or humoral immune responses.
IgM, IgG, and occasionally, IgA deposits can be found in both the pericardium and myocardium.
Serum antibody titers may be elevated with a 4-fold increase in titers suggestive but not diagnostic of viral pericarditis.
Auscultate for a pericardial rub and obtain an ECG and echocardiogram in patients with chest pain that increases with inspiration or when recumbent. C

If the ECG demonstrates diffuse ST-segment elevation without T-wave inversion and PR interval depression (except in aVR) and there is echocardiographic evidence of a pericardial effusion, the diagnosis of pericarditis is very likely. C
See topic on Chest pain for differential diagnosis.

Acute pericarditis should be considered in patients presenting with new onset chest pain that increases with inspiration or when recumbent, and is typically relieved by leaning forward. They may also report a prodrome of fever, fatigue, and myalgias.

Auscultation of a pericardial friction rub supports the diagnosis of pericarditis. Have the patient lean forward, exhale, and auscultate at the left lower sternal border while the patient inspires. In a series of 100 patients with pericardial friction rub, most had a triphasic rub, followed by biphasic and monophasic (during ventricular systole only). The rub may be palpable.

Dyspnea (87%), elevated jugular venous pressure (76%), tachycardia (77%), tachypnea, hypotension (26%), muffled heart tones (28%), and pulsus paradoxus (82%) support the diagnosis of cardiac tamponade—a life threatening but uncommon complication of acute pericarditis. In a study of 65 patients with known effusion, pulsus paradoxus more than 12 mm Hg was 98% sensitive and 83% specific for tamponade (LR+ 5.9, LR− 0.03).

ECG findings of pericarditis differ by stage (see ). Pericardial effusion is suggested by low voltage, PR segment depression, and electrical alternans. However, while specific, these findings are of limited sensitivity for either any effusion or moderate/large effusion.

Chest x-ray is also of low sensitivity for pericardial effusion. Findings include enlarged silhouette, pericardial fat stripe, predominantly left sided effusion, and increased transverse cardiac diameters.

Echocardiography usually demonstrates a small or moderate pericardial effusion and infrequently a large pericardial effusion or cardiac tamponade. Pericardial fluid, when available, should be analyzed for cytology, WBC, RBC, triglycerides, smear, and cultures.
The clinical presentation should guide the use of serologic testing as the cost-effectiveness and diagnostic value of routine testing has not been established.

Cardiac CT and MR imaging are optional and most useful when demonstrating pericardial effusion if previous tests are inconclusive for pericarditis. In patients with malignancies, CT/MRI may confirm direct or hematogenous metastases to the heart and pericardium.

Serum troponin I and creatinine kinase MB: Serum troponin I and CK-MB are elevated in 49% to 71% of patients who have acute idiopathic pericarditis and ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction and therefore are not helpful in the differentiating pericarditis from myocardial infarction. Patients in whom acute myocardial infarction is suspected should undergo coronary angiography.
Suspect pericarditis in patients with retrosternal chest discomfort that increases with inspiration or when recumbent that is accompanied by a pericardial friction rub (see ).
Order ECG, troponin, CBC, sed rate or CRP, and echocardiogram to confirm the diagnosis.

Widespread ST-segment elevation with PR interval depression on ECG and/or presence of pericardial effusion on echocardiography support the diagnosis. The absence of these findings do not exclude acute pericarditis.
WBC, sedimentation rate, and CRP are usually elevated, as is cardiac troponin in 35% to 50% of patients. Viral cultures and antibody titers are usually not useful.
NSAIDs are the preferred treatment for the first occurrence of idiopathic or viral pericarditis. A
Aspirin is the preferred treatment for the pericarditis associated with myocardial infarction. B
Colchicine combined with NSAIDs decreases recurrences among patients with acute or recurrent pericarditis, but it may lead to more adverse events and to more patients discontinuing treatment. A
Glucocorticoids should not be routinely used. A

Ibuprofen 1600 to 3200 mg daily for 1 month or colchicine 1.0 to 2.0 mg on day 1 and 0.5 to 1.0 daily for 3 months are the recommended treatments for idiopathic or viral pericarditis and results in pain relief in 85% to 90% of patients.
Aspirin 650 to 975 mg every 6 to 8 hours is the preferred treatment for pericarditis associated with myocardial infarction.

Colchicine 1.0 to 2.0 mg for 1 day followed by 0.5 to 1.0 mg daily for 3 months has been shown in an open label RCT to significantly prolong the symptom-free interval and to reduce the recurrence rate (10.7% vs. 32.3%, NNT = 5). A randomized double-blinded trial demonstrated the efficacy of colchicine (0.5-1.0 mg daily for 3 months) in limiting symptoms of acute pericariditis and reducing recurrence when used in conjunction with standard anti-inflammatory therapy. A Cochrane review found moderate quality evidence for the efficacy of colchicine combined with NSAIDs in preventing recurrences at 18 months among patients with acute or recurrent pericarditis. However, adding colchicine to standard therapy with NSAIDs may lead to more adverse events and to more patients discontinuing treatment.

Due to increased risk of recurrent pericarditis, glucocortocoids should not be routinely administered for a first episode of pericarditis unless indicated for an associated clinical condition. When necessary for recurrent pericarditis, low-dose prednisone 0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg per day has been demonstrated to be superior to high-dose prednisone 1.0 mg/kg per day (33% vs. 65% recurrence rate, NNT = 32). There is also concern that corticosteriods used to treat pericarditis after myocardial infarction may increase the risk of myocardial rupture.
When pericarditis is a manifestation of an underlying disease, therapy should be directed toward management of that disease.
Recurrent pericarditis can be effectively treated with colchicine to reduce the chance of further recurrence (NNT = 3.3 patients to prevent 1 episode over 18 month period).

Rilonacept is an interleukin 1 trap (inhibitor). In a clinical trial, 86 patients with recurrent pericarditis and c-reactive protein greater than 10 mg/L underwent an active run-in period, and the 61 responders were then randomized to rilonacept or placebo for 12 weeks. Recurrences occurred less often in the rilonacept group (7% vs 74%, p < 0.001). The study design with an active run-in period will bias the results in favor of finding an effect for the study drug.

A cohort study of 53 patients suggests that long-term rilonacept treatment beyond 18-24 months may improve remission and cessation of therapy may lead to recurrence of rericarditis in two-thirds of patients. Larger, multicenter trials with long-term followup are needed to confirm these findings.
Low-risk patients may not require hospitalization for further evaluation or treatment of pericarditis.

High-risk patients should be hospitalized. High-risk identifiers include temperature greater than 38°C, sub-acute onset, immunosuppression, trauma, oral anticoagulation, presence of myopericarditis, aspirin or NSAID failure and presence of a large pericardial effusion or tamponade.
Pericardiocentesis is indicated for very large pericardial effusions, impending cardiac tamponade or when necessary for diagnostic purposes; diagnostic yield from pericardial fluid is typically low.

Pericardiectomy should be reserved for frequent and highly symptomatic recurrent pericarditis resistant to combination medical therapy. This is not a common therapeutic approach and has significant morbidity.

Post-Pericardiotomy Syndrome: Colchicine has been shown to reduce the likelihood of post-pericardiotomy syndrome in a randomized trial with 180 patients (19% vs. 29%, p <0.05, NNT = 10), although there was no effect on the likelihood of atrial fibrillation. The value of corticosteroids to prevent post-pericardiotomy syndrome is limited and unclear.
Pericarditis is most often a self-limited disease that responds within 2 weeks to conservative management and NSAIDs. A
Large pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade, and constriction are infrequent complications of idiopathic or viral pericarditis. B
Recurrent pericarditis may be more difficult to treat than the initial episode of pericarditis. B

With the exception of pyogenic and malignant pericarditis, the course is usually benign. Patients with viral and idiopathic pericarditis usually have resolution of both symptoms and pericardial effusions within 2 weeks.
Fifteen percent to 30% of viral or idiopathic pericarditis patients have recurrent pericarditis which rarely results in cardiac tamponade or pericardial constriction.
Large pericardial effusions, which may require drainage, most often occur in pericarditis associated with neoplasm, tuberculosis, uremia, and myxedema.

A study followed 486 consecutive Italian patients with acute pericarditis (n = 346), perimycarditis (n = 26), or myopericarditis (n = 114) for a median of 36 months. Outcomes were uniformly good, with no cardiovascular deaths or heart failure. Only 8% had residual mild LV dysfunction among those originally diagnosed with myopericarditis, and only 15% among those originally diagnosed with perimyocarditis. Recurrences occured relatively often among those with acute pericarditis (32%).

For clinically stable patients with small to moderate pericardial effusion, follow-up including repeat echocardiogram is reasonable 1 to 2 weeks after initiation of therapy but should be considered earlier in patients with larger effusions.
Revaluation every 6 months is recommended for clinically stable patients.
Participation in amateur and competitive sports should be restricted for at least 3 months after onset of pericarditis.
Athletes can return to full sports activity if there is resolution of fever, absence of pericardial effusion, and normalization of serum inflammatory markers on 3 month evaluation.

Indomethacin reduces coronary blood flow by impacting prostaglandin-mediated vasoreactivity and should be avoided in the treatment of elderly patients with pericarditis due to risk of myocardial ischemia.

Recurrent pericarditis may be challenging to diagnose in older adults since they may present with less common clinical features, including frequent dyspnea, pleural effusion, severe pericardial effusion, lower fever, and lower leukocyte count. And given more comorbidities among this population, they receive much less NSAIDs, colchicine, corticosteroids, and anti-IL1 agents.

feature.caption: Differentiating Pericarditis from ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction or Pulmonary Emboli.
feature.feature_body:
Pericarditis STEMI Pulmonary Emboli
Chest Pain
Respiration Pleuritic No change Pleuritic Absent with apnea
Position Increases if supine; decreases if sitting No change No change
Location Retrosternal Retrosternal Anterior posterior lateral
Exam Pericardial rub 85% Absent Pleural friction 3%
ECG Changes
ST elevation Concave and widespread Convex and localized to a vascular distribution Limited to II, III, AFV, and V1
Q-waves Absent Usually present May be present II, III, and AFV
PR depression Frequent Rare Absent
T-wave inversion After ST segment normalized While ST segment elevated II, III, AVF, V1-V4, while ST segment elevated
STEMI denotes ST-elevation myocardial infarction.

feature.caption: Electrocardiogram Findings in Acute Pericarditis, by Stage.
feature.feature_body:
Stage ECG Findings
I Diffuse concave ST-segment elevation and PR depression without T-wave inversion
II (early) ST-segment return to baseline with persistent PR deviation
II (late) T-waves flatten and invert
III Generalized T-wave inversion
IV ECG returns to prepericarditis state
